summary:
Bulgaria criminalises neither gender identity nor gender expression, and no statute governs which public facilities a person may use on the basis of gender. Same-sex relations were decriminalised in 1968. A foreign passport is examined on ordinary terms at the border, and a recorded gender marker raises no separate question; no entry rule or screening procedure turns on a visitor's gender identity.

Legal gender recognition is closed. The Supreme Court of Cassation's interpretative decision of 20 February 2023 holds that "the only meaning of the term sex should be its biological one" and that the legal system rests on "the binary existence of humankind", which bars legal gender change. The Constitutional Court's verdict on the Istanbul Convention condemned legislation providing for legal gender recognition.

The European Court of Human Rights found in Y.T. v Bulgaria in 2020 that refusal of legal gender recognition violated Article 8, and in its December 2024 revision decision made clear that those obligations were unaffected by the 2024 registry revision, consistent with P.H. v Bulgaria. Judge Šimáčková dissented that the revision decision was over-formalistic.

External pressure on the ban is live but unresolved. In September 2025 an Advocate General of the Court of Justice of the European Union issued an opinion that EU law precludes national legislation such as Bulgaria's refusing a trans person identity documents matching their presented gender, and the court concurred with the Advocate General's proposed reasoning. The full judgment was pending.

Anti-discrimination protection is layered and incomplete. The Protection Against Discrimination Act took effect on 1 January 2004, covering direct and indirect discrimination in housing, education and healthcare, and was expanded in 2015 to cover "sex" including "sex change". Gender identity and gender expression are not explicitly named in that revision. Health services fall under the sexual-orientation discrimination ban in force since 1 January 2004.

Hate-crime law exists; enforcement is the documented failure. Amnesty International reported in February 2015 that authorities consistently fail to identify and adequately investigate bias crimes, that attacks spiked in 2013 according to the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee, and that the Sofia prosecution opened only some cases. A January 2014 government commitment to outlaw such hate crimes was dropped by the government formed after the October 2014 elections. Heavier penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation were adopted on 28 July 2023.

Documented violence includes the 2008 killing of a 25-year-old student in a Sofia park by a group intending to "cleanse" the park of gay men, and the assault in Plovdiv on 27 September 2020 of children as young as 14 or 15 by ultra-fans of the Botev football club. The first Sofia Pride in 2008, with about 150 participants, was attacked with petrol bombs, rocks and glass bottles, and more than 60 hooligans were arrested.

Public LGBT visibility is secured by police presence rather than settled tolerance. The 2011 Sofia Pride passed without incident under heavy police guard with only a "Family NGO" protest, after far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 editions. Ahead of the 10 June 2017 march, Human Rights Watch urged authorities to protect participants after the National Resistance group rallied counter-demonstrators to "cleanse Sofia from garbage".

State hostility also operates through education law. On 7 August 2024 parliament amended the education law to prohibit "propaganda, promotion, or incitement... directly or indirectly" of ideas about "non-traditional sexual orientation and/or gender identity other than the biological one", defined as attraction contrary to Bulgaria's legal concept of opposite sexes. President Rumen Radev signed it and it entered into force on 16 August 2024; the amendment was introduced by the Revival party with the backing of GERB.

At municipal level, the Pazardzhik District Council voted in November 2009 to forbid the "public demonstration of sexual or any other orientation". The Administrative Court struck it down in October 2010 for procedural errors and upheld it on appeal in July 2011.

Partner recognition is contested and inconsistent. Article 46 of the Constitution has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 1991, banning same-sex marriage; the Constitution does not prohibit civil unions, but none exist, so couples are denied inheritance, medical decision-making and joint property rights. A Sofia court granted an Australian woman and her French wife, married in France in 2016, the right to reside in Bulgaria on 29 June 2018 under the Coman ruling, after they had been refused a year earlier, and a Bulgarian court recognised a same-sex marriage performed in France in 2019. A couple married in the United Kingdom had their recognition claim rejected by the Sofia Administrative Court in January 2018, and the LGBT organisation Deystvie pursued an appeal. In September 2023 the European Court of Human Rights held that Bulgaria's refusal to recognise same-sex couples is an "infringement of human rights"; that case was subject to appeals and awaiting a government response. Same-sex couples are barred from adopting, and a 2021 Court of Justice of the European Union ruling forced Bulgaria to issue identity documents to the child of a lesbian couple after it refused a birth certificate. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under Bulgarian law, recognition depends on litigation that has gone both ways.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe ranked Bulgaria 37th of 49 European countries for LGBT rights protection in 2020.

Billboards promoting tolerance toward same-sex couples in Varna and Burgas were vandalised in December 2018, and the Bulgarian Orthodox Church calls pride events a "sinful demonstration".

Anti-LGBT rhetoric rose in 2020 and 2021, a period in which "gender became a slur"; the far-right National Resistance advocated brooms and shovels against pride attendees, and the Ataka party mounted protests.

The 1964 show trial of 26 men, including actor Georgi Partsalev and singer Emil Dimitrov, was described by experts as "a masquerade for the public" about "decadent Western culture".
localsOnly:
Intersex newborns routinely have male genitalia removed as the "easier operation", with parents "rarely informed" of later harm to the child's gender identity, and there are no laws concerning intersex people.

Single Step Foundation, founded in 2016, works with LGBTI youth on coming out and affirmation, and launched Bulgaria's first licensed online support chat in October 2017 for LGBTI youth, families and allies.

A 2008 survey of 15 schools in Sofia, Varna and Plovdiv found 10.5% of students identified as bisexual and 1.8% as gay; 29% said they would refuse to sit next to a gay classmate, 5% said they would bully gay classmates and 39% said they would protect them.

Gay and bisexual men are not explicitly barred from donating blood. The donor form, under a Ministry of Healthcare ordinance of 19 July 2004, does not ask orientation but requires confirmation of no HIV or STI-risk practices.
outOfScopeNotes:
The September 2025 Court of Justice of the European Union opinion had not produced a final judgment in the sources reviewed, so its effect on Bulgaria's recognition ban is unresolved.

The September 2023 European Court of Human Rights finding on non-recognition was subject to appeal, and a government response was awaited.

Whether the 2015 revision of the Protection Against Discrimination Act reaches gender identity and gender expression is not resolved by the sources; the amended text names "sex" including "sex change" only.

Current levels of hate-crime investigation and prosecution are not sourced here. The enforcement failure is documented in a 2015 report, and later reporting carries the pattern forward without updated figures.

The sources do not state whether the Pazardzhik municipal ban remains in force after the July 2011 appeal decision.
